**Abstract** Al, F-doped new perovskite lithium ion conductors  $\text{Li}_{3x}\text{La}_{2/3-x^{\alpha}1/3-2x}\text{Ti}_{1-y}\text{Al}_y\text{O}_{3-y}\text{F}_y$  (x=0.11) have been prepared by solid state reaction. It is found that a pure perovskite-structured phase with space group of P4mm(99) exits in the composition range of  $0 < y \le 0.10$ . The sample with y=0.02 possesses the highest ionic conductivity of  $1.06 \times 10^{-3}$  S/cm at room temperature, and its decomposing voltage is 2.3 V. The factors affecting the conductivity of this system are discussed.

**Keywords** Perovskite · Lithium fast ion conductor · LLT · Ionic conductivity · Al, F-doped

structure.title: Introduction
structure.text:
Lithium fast ion conductors are of great interest for their potential use as electrolyte of full solid-state batteries and in other electrochemical devices. Of these materials,  $\text{Li}_{3x}\text{La}_{2/3-x^{\Box}1/3-2x}\text{TiO}_3$  (LLT), where  $\Box$  represents vacancy with a perovskite-related structure, has attracted peculiar attention for its high lithium ion conductivity of  $1.0 \times 10^{-3}$  S/cm at room temperature when  $x\approx0.10$  [1]. To further improve lithium ion conductivity, much effort has been dedicated to substitute A-site La by other cations, such as other rare earth cations or alkaline earth cations, and/or substitute B-site Ti by other trivalent, tetravalent, pentavalent or hexavalent cations [2–13]. So far, only doping Sr up to 5% [12] and partial substitution of Al for Ti [10] are reported to increase the ionic conductivity slightly.

Based on these research, the ionic conductivity is proposed to depend mainly on the following factors [1, 10-13]:

- The size of the A-site cation. As lithium ion conductivity originates from the motion of lithium along the A-site vacancies, the window of four oxygens separating adjacent A sites constitute the bottleneck for lithium ion migration. Thus, La substituted by smaller ions reduces the bottleneck size and suppresses the lithium ion migration, while the substitution of larger ions increases the bottleneck size and enhances the ion migration.
- Lithium ion and vacancy concentration in the A sublattice.
- 3. Ordering or disordering of La, Li, and vacancies. The more the arrangement of their distribution is ordered, the lower the conductivity will be.
- 4. The facility of tilting of TiO<sub>6</sub> octahedra. The easier the tilting the higher the ionic conductivity.
- 5. The local structure. The local lattice distortion will increase the activation energy of ionic conductivity and will decrease the ionic conductivity.
- 6. The change of bond strength between A–O and B–O bond in ABO<sub>3</sub> perovskites. Stronger B–O bond favors high ionic conductivity.

In this study, a new perovskite solid solution with F and Al co-doped LLT were synthesized for the first time and characterized by AC impedance spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction (XRD), and DC polarization.

structure.text:
Different compositions of the  $\text{Li}_{3x}\text{La}_{2/3-x^{\text{o}}1/3-2x}\text{Ti}_{1-y}\text{Al}_y$   $O_{3-y}F_y$  (x=0.11) system were prepared from stoichiometric amounts of  $\text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3$ ,  $\text{La}_2\text{O}_3$ ,  $\text{TiO}_2$ ,  $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ , and LiF plus 5% extra weight of  $\text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3$  to compensate lithium loss at high temperature. All the reagents were dried just before use. The mixture was ground together in agate mortar until

e-mail: rongwei@fzu.edu.cn Tel.: +86-591-87893230

thoroughly blended and then transferred to Pt boats and heated at 700 °C for 4 h for decarbonation. Afterwards, the samples were reground, pelletized, covered with powder of the sample of the same composition, and fired at 1,200 °C for 25 h to finish the reaction.

The crystal structure of the product was investigated by powder X-ray diffraction in Philips X'pert Pro diffractometer using Cu K $\alpha$ 1 ( $\lambda$ =1.54056 Å) radiation at room temperature.

Electrical conductivity was measured by an AC impedance technique on reheated discs (13-mm diameter and about 2-mm thick) from room temperature to 400 °C in the frequency range of 0.1 Hz-8 MHz. The discs were prepared by pressing the powders in an evacuated die at 12 MPa and then reheating at  $\sim 1,050$  °C for about 10 h. The discs were then coated with a silver paint and dried at 100 °C, then heated at 600 °C for 30 min to put it between two silver plates to ensure a good electrode/electrolyte contact. The entire cell assembly was placed in a tubular furnace, in which the temperature could be controlled to  $\pm 2$  °C with a temperature controller (model YCC-1211) for impedance measurement. Decomposing voltage of the sample was measured by DC polarization experiment using graphite as both of the electrodes in the voltage range of 0– 4.0 V in air. All the measurements of electrochemical properties were carried out in ZAHNER Elektrik Thales IM6 Station (Germany).

To clarify the effect of F substitution, F-doped solid solution $\text{Li}_{3x-0.02}\text{La}_{0.67-x}\text{TiO}_{2.98}\text{F}_{0.02}$ was synthesized by the same method. The results of conductivity measurements show that the bulk ionic conductivity at RT is in the order of $10^{-4}$ S/cm, with the highest one of $3.17\times10^{-4}$ S/cm for x=0.11. These results indicate that doping F solely could not improve the ionic conductivity, but F substitution improves the electrochemical stability of the system. The decomposing voltage of F substitution sample is higher than that of Al,F-codoped sample, as shown in Fig. 4. Thus, Al,F-codoping increases the decomposing voltage while maintaining the high conductivity, and such material shows more potential for application. Thus, the current is kept constant at 3.0–3.3 V and resumes to increase until LiOH begins to decompose. Upon scanning the voltage from 5.00 to 0 V, the ionic current keeps decreasing until only the electronic current remains. It is found from Table 2 that the ionic conductivity fluctuates with y value, i.e., the ionic conductivity increases when y increases from 0 to 0.02, then it decreases with a further increase of the y value to 0.06. When y=0.07, the ionic conductivity reaches another peak value, after which the conductivity resumes to decrease with an increase of the y value. Since the concentration of vacancy and lithium ion does not change with the value of y in the present ![](_page_3_Figure_6.jpeg) Fig. 5 Cyclic voltammetry profile for sample of 2LTF measured in air with sample sandwiched between two graphite electrodes system $\text{Li}_{3x}\text{La}_{2/3-x^{\Box}1/3-2x}\text{Ti}_{1-y}\text{Al}_y\text{O}_{3-y}\text{F}_y$ (x=0.11), the ratio of vacancy to lithium ion, which may play a role in affecting conductivity, can be ruled out. The ordering of cations and vacancies at A site should not play a major role, as cubic superstructure reflections exit in all the samples and their strengths change slightly with the y value. To explain the changing trend of ionic conductivity, the following factors should be considered: - Size of bottleneck. If the value of y does not increase to such a degree that can distort the tetragonal structure, more Ti4+ and O2- will be replaced by smaller sized Al3+ and F- respectively, when the y value increases. This leads to the contraction of the unit-cell as we discussed previously, allowing the reduction of bottleneck size for Li+ migration and making it more difficult for TiO6 octahedra to tilt [10, 12]. Hence, the ionic conductivity will decrease, but with more Al and F being introduced to the system, the tetragonal structure will be distorted, which makes the volume of unit-cell begin to increase, and a peak value appears at y=0.07. Hence, the bottleneck size is enlarged; accordingly, the conductivity reaches another peak value at y=0.07. - The change of bond strength between A-O and B-O bond in ABO3 perovskites. It has been suggested that the bond strengths of A-O and B-O in ABO3 perovskite are competing because they use the same 2p oxygen orbitals [10, 12]. That is, the stronger the A–O bond, the weaker the B–O bond and vice versa, and the strength of an ionic bond is dominated by the interionic distance and the covalent character of the bond [10, 12]. The shorter the interionic distance, the stronger the ionic bond [10, 12]. When smaller Al3+ replaces Ti4+, the B-O bond will be shortened. Hence, the B-O bond will be strengthened, weakening the Li-O bond, and the mobility of Li+ will be enhanced. On the other hand, the polarizing ability of Al3+ is slightly weaker than that of Ti4+ and Al doping will enhance the ionic character of B-O bond, i.e., enhance the B-O bond and weaken the Li-O bond. As a consequence, the conductivity increases from y=0 to y=0.02. - 3. F is the most electronegative element. The bond between F and other metal elements is mainly of ionic character since the charge of F- is only half of O2-. The electrostatic force between cations and F- will be nearly half of that between cations and O2- since the charge of B-site cations is much higher than that of Li+. The degree of absolute weakening of B-F bond compared to B-O bond is much larger than that of Li-F bond compared to Li-O bond. Thus, F substitution will enhance the competitiveness of Li-F bond, i.e., strengthen the Li-F bond relatively. Thus, the mobility of Li+ will be weakened and the ionic conductivity will decrease as a result. Mainly because of the co-impact of the aforementioned factors, the ionic conductivity shows the fluctuating trend along the *y* value.

nodes.text: To clarify the effect of F substitution, F-doped solid solution  $\text{Li}_{3x-0.02}\text{La}_{0.67-x}\text{TiO}_{2.98}\text{F}_{0.02}$  was synthesized by the same method. These results indicate that doping F solely could not improve the ionic conductivity, but F substitution improves the electrochemical stability of the system. The decomposing voltage of F substitution sample is higher than that of Al,F-codoped sample, as shown in Fig. 4. Thus, Al,F-codoping increases the decomposing voltage while maintaining the high conductivity, and such material shows more potential for application.

nodes.text: To see what will happen when the voltage scans back to 0 V, cyclic voltammetry measurement for sample of 2 LTF between 0–5.0 V was taken. The profile is shown in Fig. 5. When the voltage is lower than 2.0 V, the current is low and exhibits a linear relationship with voltage. Such a low current is mainly contributed by the electronic current and small part of the ionic current. Once the voltage is higher than 2.0 V, the current deviates from the linear relationship, then increases sharply when the voltage is higher than 2.3 V, indicating that the sample started to decompose and lithium ion was reduced to lithium on the interface of the cathode and the sample.

nodes.title: Factors Affecting Conductivity: Bottleneck Size
nodes.text:
To explain the changing trend of ionic conductivity, the following factors should be considered:

- Size of bottleneck. If the value of y does not increase to such a degree that can distort the tetragonal structure, more Ti<sup>4+</sup> and O<sup>2-</sup> will be replaced by smaller sized Al<sup>3+</sup> and F<sup>-</sup> respectively, when the y value increases. This leads to the contraction of the unit-cell as we discussed previously, allowing the reduction of bottleneck size for Li<sup>+</sup> migration and making it more difficult for TiO<sub>6</sub> octahedra to tilt [10, 12]. Hence, the ionic conductivity will decrease, but with more Al and F being introduced to the system, the tetragonal structure will be distorted, which makes the volume of unit-cell begin to increase, and a peak value appears at y=0.07. Hence, the bottleneck size is enlarged; accordingly, the conductivity reaches another peak value at y=0.07.

nodes.title: Factors Affecting Conductivity: Bond Strength (Al Substitution)
nodes.text:
- The change of bond strength between A-O and B-O bond in ABO<sub>3</sub> perovskites. It has been suggested that the bond strengths of A-O and B-O in ABO<sub>3</sub> perovskite are competing because they use the same 2p oxygen orbitals [10, 12]. That is, the stronger the A–O bond, the weaker the B–O bond and vice versa, and the strength of an ionic bond is dominated by the interionic distance and the covalent character of the bond [10, 12]. The shorter the interionic distance, the stronger the ionic bond [10, 12]. When smaller Al<sup>3+</sup> replaces Ti<sup>4+</sup>, the B-O bond will be shortened. Hence, the B-O bond will be strengthened, weakening the Li-O bond, and the mobility of Li<sup>+</sup> will be enhanced. On the other hand, the polarizing ability of Al<sup>3+</sup> is slightly weaker than that of Ti<sup>4+</sup> and Al doping will enhance the ionic character of B-O bond, i.e., enhance the B-O bond and weaken the Li-O bond. As a consequence, the conductivity increases from y=0 to y=0.02.
- 3.

structure.title: **Conclusion**
structure.text:
Al,F-doped perovskite lithium ion conductors  $\text{Li}_{3x}$   $\text{La}_{2/3-x^{\text{o}}1/3-2x}\text{Ti}_{1-y}\text{Al}_y\text{O}_{3-y}\text{F}_y$  (x=0.11) have been synthesized. Al substitution enhances the ionic conductivity, while F substitution improves the electrochemical stability. The sample with the initial composition of y=0.02 possesses the best conductivity of  $1.06\times10^{-3}$  S/cm at RT, and its decomposing voltage is 2.3 V. Though from thermodynamic point of view, LLT-based lithium ion conductors cannot be used as electrolyte for batteries using Li as anode [16]. It could be used as electrolyte in lithium ion batteries with open circuit voltage lower then 2.3 V.
